title: SEVEN WOMEN WILL BEG ONE MAN TO GIVE THEM HIS NAME—BUT THE REASON IS MORE TERRIFYING THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: SEVEN WOMEN WILL BEG ONE MAN TO GIVE THEM HIS NAME—BUT THE REASON IS MORE TERRIFYING THAN YOU THINK

Isaiah 4:1 reveals a desperate scene of shame, judgment, and survival. But what happens when we follow the prophecy into the next verses reveals something far greater: the difference between desperately wanting a name to cover our disgrace and receiving the grace of the One who can truly wash it away.
Imagine a world where seven women approach one man.
Not because he is wealthy.
Not because he is handsome.
Not because they have fallen in love with him.
But because they are desperate for something he possesses.
His name.
They are willing to feed themselves. Clothe themselves. Carry their own expenses. They are not even asking him to provide for them.
They just want him to take away their disgrace.
And the most unsettling part?
God Himself revealed this scene through the prophet Isaiah.
Listen carefully to the words:
“And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.” — Isaiah 4:1, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
“Only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.”
They are not pleading for affection.
They are pleading for acceptance.
And perhaps that is where this ancient prophecy begins to touch something painfully familiar in the human heart.
Because sometimes, the thing we desperately want from another person is not even love.
It is the assurance that we are no longer someone to be ashamed of.
But before we turn this prophecy into a message about our own lives, we must understand what God was actually saying.
Because Isaiah 4:1 is not a romantic prophecy about seven women marrying one extraordinary man.
It is not a secret prediction that seven women will literally marry Jesus.
And it is not permission to turn a passage about judgment into a sensational teaching about marriage.
The truth is far more sobering.
And when understood in its proper context, far more powerful.
Isaiah was speaking to Judah and Jerusalem during a time of spiritual rebellion, social injustice, arrogance, and coming judgment.
The people had become confident in their outward appearance while their inward condition was collapsing.
Their society had learned how to display prosperity without practicing righteousness.
They knew how to look impressive.
But they were forgetting how to walk humbly before God.
Isaiah 3 describes corrupt leadership, oppression, pride, and the devastating consequences of covenant unfaithfulness.
Then comes a terrifying warning.
“Thy men shall fall by the sword, and thy mighty in the war.” — Isaiah 3:25, KJV
Suddenly, Isaiah 4:1 begins to make sense.

The prophet portrays a future in which warfare and judgment have devastated the male population so severely that women are desperately seeking the security and social standing associated with marriage.
In the ancient society being addressed, remaining unmarried could carry considerable social stigma, particularly when accompanied by insecurity and the loss of family protection.
The women in Isaiah's prophecy offer to provide their own food and clothing because they are not primarily negotiating financial support.
They are pleading for the removal of reproach.
The Hebrew makes this especially striking.
The phrase translated “seven women” is שֶׁבַע נָשִׁים — sheva nashim.
And “one man” is אִישׁ אֶחָד — ish echad.
Seven women.
One man.

The number seven may intensify the picture of desperation, but the passage does not establish that exactly seven women must someday marry one particular man. The prophetic image communicates a devastating imbalance following judgment.
Then comes the heartbreaking request:
אֲסֹף חֶרְפָּתֵנוּ — esof cherpatenu.
“Take away our reproach.”
The Hebrew word cherpah carries the sense of reproach, disgrace, or shame.
This is not a casual request.
It is a cry from people whose circumstances have left them exposed to humiliation.
They are effectively saying:
We will take care of everything else.
Just let us carry your name.
And that is where the story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because although Isaiah was describing a specific prophetic judgment, the desire to escape shame is something human beings still understand.
Some people spend their entire lives trying to make their names respectable.
They build careers so nobody will remember where they came from.
They collect achievements so nobody will notice how empty they feel.
They enter relationships because being chosen feels like proof that they are valuable.
They post smiling photographs while privately wondering whether anyone would stay if they knew the truth.
And some even become deeply involved in church activities because they are afraid of what would happen if someone discovered how much they are struggling.
They know the songs.
They know when to raise their hands.
They know how to say, “God is good.”
But when the worship service ends and the room becomes quiet, they still hear the accusations.
You failed.
You ruined everything.
You should have known better.
If people knew what you did, they would never look at you the same way.
And perhaps the most exhausting part of carrying shame is that you eventually begin to believe it is your identity.
Not merely something you have done.
Something you are.
But there is a difference between the Holy Spirit convicting us of sin and shame convincing us that redemption is impossible.
Conviction calls us to repentance and directs us toward Christ.
Condemnation tells us there is no reason to return.
And the Gospel announces something that shame desperately wants us to forget.
Jesus Christ did not come to make sin look respectable. He came to save sinners.
Now watch what happens when we continue reading Isaiah.
Because if we stop at verse one, we leave the reader standing in the ruins.
But the prophet does not stop there.
Immediately after the image of humiliation and desperation, Isaiah announces something extraordinary.
“In that day shall the branch of the LORD be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and comely for them that are escaped of Israel.” — Isaiah 4:2, KJV
Did you catch that?
The same prophetic passage that begins with desperate people seeking a human name turns toward the beauty and glory of the LORD's Branch.
The Hebrew expression is צֶמַח יְהוָה — tsemach YHWH.
“The Branch of the LORD.”

Within Isaiah's immediate context, this language announces restoration and flourishing after judgment. Christians also recognize a broader biblical pattern in which the promised righteous Branch is associated with the coming Messiah, especially in Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 3:8.
We should not pretend that Isaiah 4:2 explicitly identifies Jesus by name.
But reading the Scriptures in the light of their fulfillment in Christ, we see the hope of God's ultimate restoration coming into focus.
The story does not end with human disgrace.
It moves toward divine restoration.
And this matters because the Bible does not merely tell us that people are ashamed.
It tells us what God does about sin and uncleanness.
Isaiah 4:4 speaks of the Lord washing away the filth of Zion's daughters and cleansing Jerusalem through judgment and purification.
This is not sentimental language.
God's holiness is not negotiable.
He does not restore His people by pretending their rebellion never happened.
He deals with evil.
He exposes what is corrupt.
He purifies what has become defiled.
And centuries later, the New Testament reveals the breathtaking cost of our redemption.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, bore our sins on the cross.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because His mercy is greater than the guilt of everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
Think about the difference.
In Isaiah 4:1, the women are desperate for a man's name to remove their social disgrace.
In the Gospel, sinners receive something infinitely greater than borrowed respectability.
They are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The name of another human being might change how society treats you.
But only Jesus can reconcile you to the Father.
And there is a woman in the New Testament whose story makes this truth almost impossible to forget.
She was brought before Jesus in public.
Not celebrated.
Not protected.
Exposed.
The religious leaders presented her as a woman caught in adultery.
Her sin had become the center of everyone's attention.
The crowd was ready to condemn.
The accusers were ready to use her case to test Jesus.
And she stood there with nowhere to hide.

John 8:1–11, a passage whose manuscript history is debated and which is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, preserves this familiar account of the woman brought before Jesus. Its portrayal of mercy and the call to leave sin is consistent with teachings clearly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
Jesus did not declare adultery righteous.
He did not tell her that repentance was unnecessary.
But neither did He join the crowd in treating her as disposable.
After her accusers departed, He told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Mercy.
And holiness.
In the same encounter.
That is the Gospel-shaped truth we must never separate.
Grace is not God giving us permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings salvation and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Jesus does not merely cover our public embarrassment.
He calls us out of the darkness that produced it.
And if you have ever wondered whether God could still receive someone with your history, listen to what the apostle Paul wrote:
“Such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Such were some of you.
Not such must you always remain.
Not such is your permanent identity.
Such were some of you.
That single word carries the testimony of lives transformed by grace.
There were people in the early church with histories of sexual immorality, idolatry, greed, drunkenness, and other sins.
Paul did not rewrite their past to make it appear innocent.
He pointed to what God had done.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
And notice that phrase.
“In the name.”
In Isaiah, desperate women wanted to be called by a man's name to remove their reproach.
In the New Testament, the saving significance of Jesus' name is not a matter of social prestige but of His person, authority, and redeeming work.
The Greek text of 1 Corinthians 6:11 includes:
ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
En tō onomati tou kyriou Iēsou Christou.
“In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.”
What a glorious difference.
Human beings can give us recognition.
Jesus gives salvation.
Human beings may accept us because of what they believe about our reputation.
Jesus knows the truth about us and still calls sinners to come to Him.
Human approval can disappear overnight.
But the promises of God in Christ do not collapse when public opinion changes.
Perhaps you know what it means to be labeled by your worst moment.
The divorce.
The addiction.
The affair.
The betrayal.
The prison sentence.
The years you wasted.
The child you disappointed.
The marriage you damaged.
The secret nobody knows.
Or perhaps your deepest pain is not something you did.
Perhaps it is something someone did to you.
You were abandoned.
Humiliated.
Rejected.
Made to feel unwanted.
And somewhere along the way, you began carrying someone else's cruelty as though it were your own identity.
Hear this carefully.
Being wounded by another person's sin does not make you guilty of their wrongdoing.
And having a sinful past does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's forgiveness.
The Gospel speaks to both the wounded and the guilty, though their needs and responsibilities are not identical.
For the wounded, there is comfort, truth, justice, and healing in the Lord.
For the guilty, there is a call to confession, repentance, restitution where appropriate, and trust in the mercy of Christ.
And for everyone who belongs to Jesus, there is a new identity rooted not in human applause but in God's grace.
John 1:12 says:
“But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.” — KJV
This is not merely a new reputation.
It is the privilege of becoming God's children through faith in Christ.
And perhaps this is the moment when the message stops being about seven women in an ancient prophecy.
And becomes about the person reading these words.
Because you may not be asking anyone to marry you to remove your shame.
But what are you asking to save you?
A promotion?
A relationship?
A bigger bank account?
A respectable family name?
A perfect church attendance record?
A public image that convinces everyone you have your life together?
What is the thing you believe will finally make you acceptable?
And what happens if you get it and still feel empty?
That is the tragedy of trying to solve a spiritual problem with a human title.
There is nothing inherently wrong with marriage, employment, achievement, or a good reputation.
These can be gifts from God.
But none of them can accomplish what only the Savior can do.
You can change your surname and still carry unforgiven sin.
You can change your address and still carry a troubled conscience.
You can change your social circle and still remain far from God.
You can change the way people describe you without ever being changed in the deepest place of your soul.
But when Jesus saves a person, something greater than public rehabilitation begins.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That does not mean every earthly consequence instantly disappears.
A forgiven person may still need to rebuild trust.
A repentant person may still need to make amends.
A healed relationship may still require time, honesty, and boundaries.
And some consequences may remain for a lifetime.
But those consequences do not have the authority to overturn God's verdict of justification for those who are in Christ.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
Not because they never sinned.
But because Christ has accomplished what they could never accomplish for themselves.
And this brings us to the question that may matter more than anything else in this entire article.
Are you trying to get people to stop being ashamed of you while refusing to bring your sin honestly before God?
Because there is a kind of religious life that looks clean from a distance and is quietly collapsing inside.
You can know Bible verses without surrendering your heart.
You can defend Christian doctrine while secretly nurturing bitterness.
You can speak about forgiveness while refusing to repent.
You can share inspirational posts every morning and spend every night imprisoned by habits you will not confront.
But Jesus did not die to help us become more convincing actors.
He died and rose again to redeem us.
And repentance is not a performance designed to earn His love.
It is the fitting response of a sinner turning toward the Savior who alone can save.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing something in your life right now, do not bury it beneath another excuse.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it to God.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Ask for wise, trustworthy help if you are trapped in a destructive pattern.
And believe the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
You do not need to invent a more respectable version of yourself before coming to Jesus.
You need to come to Him truthfully.
Brokenness is not a currency with which we purchase salvation.
Tears do not pay for sin.
Religious activity does not purchase forgiveness.
And money certainly cannot buy the favor of God.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
That is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
The sinner does not purchase redemption.
Christ has paid the price.
And the person who receives His grace is called into a new life of love, obedience, gratitude, and good works.
Maybe you are reading this while sitting alone.
Maybe your family believes you are doing fine.
Maybe everyone thinks you have already moved on from the thing that still makes you cry.
Maybe you have been carrying a secret prayer for years:
Lord, please don't let my story end like this.
And perhaps that is why these words found you today.
Not because Isaiah 4:1 secretly predicts your personal circumstances.
But because the same Scriptures that faithfully expose human pride and judgment also reveal the Lord's power to restore.
You are not required to pretend that the ruins are beautiful.
You are invited to trust the Redeemer who can bring life where sin has brought devastation.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, you can turn to Him today.
You can pray honestly:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, cleanse me, and teach me to follow You. I surrender my life to You. Let my identity no longer be ruled by shame, pride, or the approval of people, but by Your truth and grace. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula.
The invitation is to genuine repentance and faith in the living Christ.
And if you already belong to Jesus but have wandered far from Him, do not mistake your distance for proof that He has stopped calling you to return.
Come back.
Not to a performance.
Not to a religious image.
To Christ.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending they have never struggled.
But to keep pointing broken, growing, imperfect people to the perfect Savior.
To remind believers that Scripture matters.
That truth matters.
That repentance matters.
That sound doctrine matters.
And that grace is not a license to remain unchanged but the gift of God that leads us into a transformed life.
If this message has reached a place in your heart you have been afraid to acknowledge, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to share.
But sometimes, a small, honest response becomes the beginning of a much-needed conversation about faith, repentance, and hope.
And please do not keep this message to yourself.
Someone who never comments on your posts may read every word.
Someone who has stopped attending church may discover a reason to open the Bible again.
Someone who thinks Christianity is only for respectable people may finally understand that Jesus came to call sinners to repentance.
Return to Isaiah 3 and 4.
Read the entire prophecy.
Let the contrast between judgment and restoration settle deeply into your understanding.
Then read 1 Corinthians 6, Romans 8, and 2 Corinthians 5.
Do not settle for a powerful emotional moment when God has given us His Word to shape an entire lifetime.
Every day is another opportunity to grow in Scripture, to confront sin with humility, to receive encouragement, and to become more deeply rooted in the Gospel.
And for those who believe in this mission and want to help sustain and expand it, I want to extend a personal invitation.

It is a voluntary act of partnership that helps support the continuing work of producing biblical articles, devotionals, Christian teaching, discipleship materials, and resources intended to strengthen believers and reach people who still need to hear the Gospel.
Some believers may consider it within their personal giving budget alongside their tithes and offerings, according to their convictions and the teaching of their local church.
But it is important to say this clearly.
And your love for Jesus is not measured by whether you can afford a monthly contribution.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the spirit of this invitation.
Not guilt.
Not spiritual pressure.
Grateful partnership.
It is the opportunity to participate in work that seeks to nourish faith, strengthen discipleship, and keep the message of Jesus Christ before people who desperately need it.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers grow deeper in Jesus Christ through biblical truth, spiritual encouragement, and lifelong learning.
Pray for this ministry.
Invite people to read Scripture.
Encourage someone who has lost hope.
Help someone find a faithful local church.
Show the compassion of Christ to a person who feels forgotten.
It is to see people pointed toward Jesus.
To see the spiritually weary strengthened.
To see sinners called to repentance.
To see believers equipped to understand God's Word.
To see families encouraged.
To see wounded hearts reminded that Christ is merciful.
And to see the Gospel proclaimed without compromise.
Now, before you leave, remember the women in Isaiah 4:1.
Seven women.
One man.
A desperate plea.
“Only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.”
It was a prophetic picture of judgment, devastation, and social disgrace.
But it is not the final word of Isaiah's message.
Beyond the ruins, the prophet spoke of the LORD's Branch, cleansing, holiness, and divine protection.
And through the fullness of Scripture, we are directed to the One in whom our greatest hope is found.
Jesus Christ.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls us to repent and believe.
The One who gives His people a hope that no human reputation could ever secure.
So stop asking the world to give you an identity that only God can establish.
Stop confusing public approval with spiritual peace.
Stop believing that your worst moment must become the final definition of your life.
Come to Jesus.
Not because your past was harmless.
Not because your wounds are imaginary.
Not because repentance is easy.
But because His grace is real.
His cross is sufficient.
His resurrection is true.
And His invitation still stands.
The world may remember the name attached to your scandal, but in Christ, your scandal does not have to write the ending of your story.
